questions.q: What is the determinant test result for u = [1, 2] and v = [3, 4], and what does it mean?
options: Determinant is -2 (nonzero), so the set is linearly independent
Determinant is 0, so the set is linearly dependent
Determinant is 2, so the vectors are equal
Determinants only apply to 3x3 matrices, so this test doesn't work here
questions.explain: (1)(4) - (2)(3) = 4 - 6 = -2, which is nonzero, so {[1,2],[3,4]} is linearly independent.

options: Because [2, 4] is exactly 2 times [1, 2], making the determinant zero and the second vector redundant
Because both vectors have positive entries
Because the vectors have different lengths
Because [1, 2] and [2, 4] span all of R^2 together
questions.explain: [2,4] = 2*[1,2], so the determinant (1)(4)-(2)(2) = 0, and the two vectors lie on the same line through the origin -- together they span only that line, not all of R^2.

questions.q: What is the computational basis for a single qubit?
options: {|0>, |1>}, corresponding to [1,0] and [0,1] in C^2
Any arbitrary pair of normalized vectors
A basis that only exists for multi-qubit systems, not single qubits
questions.explain: The computational basis is the standard basis of C^2, written in quantum notation as |0> = [1,0] and |1> = [0,1].

questions.q: For u=[1,0,1], v=[0,1,1], w=[1,1,0] in R^3, the 3x3 determinant works out to -2. What does this confirm?
options: The three vectors are linearly independent and form a valid basis for R^3
The three vectors are linearly dependent
The three vectors all point in the same direction
The determinant must always be positive for independent vectors, so this result is invalid
questions.explain: A nonzero determinant (-2 here) for n vectors in R^n means they are linearly independent, so this set spans all of R^3 and qualifies as a basis.

questions.q: Why does a dependent set of vectors fail to qualify as a basis, even if it technically spans a space?
options: A dependent set contains at least one redundant vector that adds no new reachable direction, so it either fails to span the full space or fails the independence requirement
A basis is only defined for spaces larger than R^2
Dependent sets always contain the zero vector
A basis must contain at least 3 vectors regardless of the space's dimension
questions.explain: A basis requires both spanning the space AND linear independence; a dependent set has at least one vector that's a combination of the others, violating the independence requirement even if the remaining vectors still span something.
